building.name: Hobart Building
building.completed_conflict: The assessor's roll gives 1922; the building opened in 1914.

historical_record.description: The Crown Zellerbach Building, completed 1959 to a Skidmore, Owings & Merrill design in the "Miesian" International Style, and designated City Landmark No. 183 in 1987 at the age of 28.

The first Hobart Building went up here, a five-storey polychrome Victorian Gothic office block by Edward R. Swain, better known as the Pacific Postal Telegraph Building after its ground-floor tenant; the Hobart estate's mining and lumber companies, the City of Paris and the Central and Southern Pacific railroads had offices in it.

With the floors of the old building partly caved in by the earthquake, the Pacific Postal Telegraph operators stayed at their keys and had sent the first news of the disaster to New York by 5:30 in the morning. The gutted building stood empty until it was pulled down by 1913.

In a dispute over fireproofing the steel floor beams, Willis Polk defied a city inspector by riding a girder up to the tenth floor of the unfinished building to await arrest, and in May hung a painted sign on it questioning Mayor Rolph's integrity, until the Hobart Estate Company quieted the row.

The Hobart Building opened late in the year, ahead of schedule and under budget: Willis Polk's 21-storey, 285-foot steel-frame tower, then the second-tallest building in San Francisco, on the site of the estate's earlier building. The City Planning Commission had made Polk drop the clock tower from his design before approving the plans in June 1913.
The building next door to the west was demolished, exposing the plain west wall that Polk never meant to be seen.

The two-storey shopfront at the west end of the Market Street front was remodelled in white marble for the Financial Savings and Loan, replacing the original pink Tennessee marble; the present shopfront dates from 1995.
Determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in a federal Section 106 review, as one of the finest historic commercial buildings in San Francisco.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places as an early San Francisco skyscraper and a major work of Willis Polk.
